platforms.title: PSA Test: 5 Facts to Weigh Before You Say Yes
platforms.meta_description: Should you get a PSA test? A high PSA often isn't cancer, the benefit is small, and US and UK advice is to decide yourself. 5 facts from USPSTF and NHS.
platforms.body_html:
You go in for a routine physical, and the doctor asks whether you want a PSA added to your blood work. It sounds like a free extra: one more tube, and you find out whether you have prostate cancer. It does not quite work that way. A PSA result is a clue that needs follow-up, not a yes-or-no cancer test, and the official advice in the US and the UK is not to test everyone, but to make the decision yourself after hearing the trade-offs. Here are five things worth knowing before you say yes.

1. A high number often has nothing to do with cancer

PSA, or prostate-specific antigen, is a protein made by the prostate. The US Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF), the independent panel that sets screening recommendations, notes that a raised level can come from cancer but also from an enlarged prostate (benign prostatic hyperplasia) or an inflamed prostate (prostatitis). Most men flagged by a single test turn out not to have cancer. In the European screening trial ERSPC, about 1 in 6 men screened at least once had one or more false-positive results, and two-thirds of the positive results in the first round were false alarms. In the US PLCO trial, more than two-thirds of men biopsied after a positive PSA did not have prostate cancer.

2. What you do in the two days before matters

The NHS tells men not to ejaculate, have anal sex, ride a bike or do exercise that leaves them out of breath for 48 hours before a PSA test, because these can raise the level and make the result less accurate. Eating and drinking as usual is fine. If you have a urine infection, the NHS says to wait 4 to 6 weeks after it clears before testing. A raised result is usually repeated before anyone talks about a biopsy or an MRI scan.

3. What screening buys you, and what it costs

The benefit is real but small. According to the USPSTF review of the large trials, PSA screening in men aged 55 to 69 may prevent about 1.3 deaths from prostate cancer per 1,000 men screened over roughly 13 years, and about 3 cases of cancer that has spread. The trials have not shown that screening reduces deaths from all causes.

The costs show up more often. Follow-up of the large trials suggests that, of men diagnosed through screening, 20% to 50% may be overdiagnosed: their cancer would never have caused symptoms in their lifetime. In the same review, about 1% of prostate biopsies led to complications needing a hospital stay. Treatment carries lasting effects: about 1 in 5 men who have the prostate removed develop long-term urinary incontinence, and about 2 in 3 have long-term erectile dysfunction. This is why many men with low-risk cancer now choose active surveillance, regular checks instead of surgery or radiation, with the option to treat if the cancer changes.

4. Your risk changes the math

The USPSTF names older age, African American race and a family history of prostate cancer as the most important risk factors. In the US, African American men are more likely to develop prostate cancer than white men (203.5 vs 121.9 cases per 100,000) and more than twice as likely to die of it. For men whose father or brother had advanced prostate cancer, spread to other organs, or died of it, the task force says screening is probably most likely to help. In the UK, the NHS does not routinely offer PSA testing, except to men whose genetic tests have shown a faulty BRCA2 gene, but any man can ask a GP to discuss it.

5. What happens when you decide with the numbers

The USPSTF's 2018 recommendation, which is currently being updated, is that for men aged 55 to 69, the decision to have periodic PSA screening should be an individual one, made after talking through benefits and harms with a clinician. It recommends against routine PSA screening at 70 and older, because the chance of benefit falls while false positives, biopsy complications and overdiagnosis rise. It also says clinicians should not screen men who have not said they want it. When you weigh your own risk, how you would feel about living with a slow cancer, and how much the treatment side effects would matter to you, the test stops being an automatic add-on and becomes your decision.

So, should you get a PSA test?

Back to that blood form. If you are between 55 and 69, it is a reasonable choice either way, and the right answer depends on your risk and your values more than on the test itself. If you are 70 or older with no symptoms, the evidence leans against routine testing. Symptoms are a different matter: the NHS lists peeing more often, a sudden urge to pee or getting up often at night, blood in your pee, and problems getting or keeping an erection as reasons to see a doctor, and a PSA test may be part of that check. Blood in your urine always needs prompt medical attention.

One small step to take before your next physical: write down whether your father or brothers had prostate cancer, and at what age, then ask your clinician what that means for you before agreeing to the extra tube. This article is general health information and does not replace advice from a clinician who knows your history.

Sources: USPSTF, "Prostate Cancer: Screening" final recommendation statement (May 2018); NHS, "PSA test" (reviewed September 2024).
